subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If m, n are integers and x = cos α + i sin α, y = cos β + i sin β, then prove that xᵐyⁿ + 1/(xᵐyⁿ) = 2cos(mα + nβ) and xᵐyⁿ − 1/(xᵐyⁿ) = 2i sin(mα + nβ).

mark_split.label: Powers of x and y by De Moivre's theorem

Re-derived: xᵐyⁿ = cis(mα + nβ) and its reciprocal is the conjugate, so the sum is 2cos(mα + nβ) and the difference 2i sin(mα + nβ); the book's answer is correct. m and n are integers, which is the case De Moivre's theorem covers exactly.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove both results — what De Moivre's theorem gives for xᵐ and yⁿ, what the product and its reciprocal are, and what adding and subtracting give.
insider_note: Four of the seven marks are the last two lines, one addition and one subtraction of the same pair. The mark most often dropped is the reciprocal, 1/cis θ = cis(−θ), and the i must stay in the second answer: 2i sin(mα + nβ).

steps.label: Powers of x and y by De Moivre
steps.margin_note: First mark. xᵐ = cos mα + i sin mα and yⁿ = cos nβ + i sin nβ. The exponent m belongs to α and n to β; write both lines before multiplying anything.
steps.memory_tip: The exponent m belongs to α and n to β. Write both powers before multiplying anything.
lines: x = cos α + i sin α = cis α,
y = cos β + i sin β = cis β
xᵐ = (cos α + i sin α)ᵐ = cos mα + i sin mα
yⁿ = (cos β + i sin β)ⁿ = cos nβ + i sin nβ
(by De Moivre's theorem, m and n integers)

recall.must_convey: That De Moivre's theorem gives xᵐ = cis mα and yⁿ = cis nβ.
accept: by De Moivre x to the m is cos m alpha plus i sin m alpha and y to the n is cis n beta
raise x to m and y to n using De Moivre so the angles become m alpha and n beta
x power m is cis m alpha and y power n is cis n beta
De Moivre tho x power m cis m alpha, y power n cis n beta avuthai
the powers multiply the angles by m and by n

steps.why: De Moivre's theorem is the only tool in the question: it moves the integer power onto the angle. Both powers are written before anything is multiplied.
common_mistakes: Writing xᵐ = cosᵐ α + i sinᵐ α, which is false.
Multiplying the angle by n for x and by m for y, swapping the exponents.
Skipping this line and writing xᵐyⁿ directly, which loses the method mark.

steps.label: The product xᵐyⁿ
steps.margin_note: Second mark. cis mα · cis nβ = cis(mα + nβ): both moduli are 1, so only the angles combine, and they add. Label it (1).
steps.memory_tip: cis mα · cis nβ = cis(mα + nβ). Both moduli are 1, so only the angles combine, and they add.
lines: xᵐyⁿ = cis mα · cis nβ = cis(mα + nβ)

recall.must_convey: That multiplying cis mα by cis nβ adds the angles, so xᵐyⁿ = cis(mα + nβ), called equation (1).
accept: multiply the two and the angles add so x m y n is cis of m alpha plus n beta
cis m alpha times cis n beta is cis m alpha plus n beta, that is equation one
the product has angle m alpha plus n beta
rendu multiply cheste angles add ayyi cis m alpha plus n beta vasthundi
equation one is cos of m alpha plus n beta plus i sin of the same

steps.why: cis A · cis B = cis(A + B) is the product rule for numbers on the unit circle: moduli multiply (1 × 1) and amplitudes add. It turns the product into a single cis.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the angles instead of adding them.
Expanding the product with four trigonometric terms and never using the product rule.
Writing the angle as mα · nβ.

steps.label: The reciprocal 1/(xᵐyⁿ)
steps.margin_note: Third mark. 1/cis(mα + nβ) = cis(−(mα + nβ)), because cis θ · cis(−θ) = cis 0 = 1. Only the sine changes sign; label it (2).
steps.memory_tip: 1/cis θ = cis(−θ), since cis θ · cis(−θ) = cis 0 = 1. Only the sine changes sign.

recall.must_convey: That the reciprocal of cis(mα + nβ) is cis(−(mα + nβ)) = cos(mα + nβ) − i sin(mα + nβ), called equation (2).
accept: the reciprocal is cis of minus the angle so cos m alpha plus n beta minus i sin, equation two
one over x m y n is the conjugate, cos minus i sin of m alpha plus n beta
taking the reciprocal changes the sign of the angle
reciprocal teeste angle minus avuthundi, cos minus i sin vasthundi
equation two is the same with a minus before the i sin

steps.why: 1/cis θ = cis(−θ) because cis θ · cis(−θ) = cis 0 = 1. For a number of modulus 1 the reciprocal is the conjugate, so only the sign of the sine changes.
common_mistakes: Writing 1/cis θ as cos θ + i sin θ with no sign change.
Changing the sign of the cosine as well as the sine.
Rationalising the fraction from scratch and losing time.

steps.label: Add (1) and (2)
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. Adding (1) and (2) cancels the sines and doubles the cosine: 2cos(mα + nβ). The angle stays whole — it does not split into 2cos mα + 2cos nβ.
steps.memory_tip: Adding cancels the sines: 2cos(mα + nβ). The angle stays whole, never splitting into two cosines.

recall.must_convey: That adding equations (1) and (2) cancels the i sin terms and gives xᵐyⁿ + 1/(xᵐyⁿ) = 2cos(mα + nβ).
accept: add one and two, the sine terms cancel and we get two cos of m alpha plus n beta
adding gives twice the real part which is two cos m alpha plus n beta
one plus two is two cos of m alpha plus n beta, the first result
rendu add cheste sin cancel ayyi two cos m alpha plus n beta vasthundi
the sum of a number and its conjugate is two times the real part

steps.why: A number of modulus 1 plus its reciprocal is the number plus its conjugate, which is twice the real part. That is the whole content of the first identity.
common_mistakes: Leaving a stray i in the sum.
Writing the result as cos(mα + nβ) without the 2.

steps.label: Subtract (2) from (1)
steps.margin_note: Sixth and seventh marks. Subtracting (2) from (1) cancels the cosines and doubles the imaginary part: 2i sin(mα + nβ). The i stays in the answer, and the order matters — (2) minus (1) gives the opposite sign.
steps.memory_tip: Subtracting leaves 2i sin(mα + nβ). The i stays, and the order (1) − (2) fixes the sign.

recall.must_convey: That subtracting equation (2) from (1) cancels the cosines and gives xᵐyⁿ − 1/(xᵐyⁿ) = 2i sin(mα + nβ).
accept: subtract two from one, the cosines cancel and we get two i sin of m alpha plus n beta
subtracting gives twice the imaginary part so two i sin m alpha plus n beta
one minus two is two i sin of m alpha plus n beta, the second result
one nunchi two subtract cheste cos cancel ayyi two i sin vasthundi
the difference of a number and its conjugate is two i times the imaginary part

steps.why: A number minus its conjugate is 2i times the imaginary part. The i stays in the answer, which is why the second identity has 2i sin and not 2 sin.
common_mistakes: Dropping the i and writing 2 sin(mα + nβ).
Subtracting (1) from (2) and getting −2i sin, the wrong sign.
Writing 2i sin(mα) − 2i sin(nβ), splitting the angle.
